sections.b: Habakkuk is a short book of three chapters set in Judah in the years when Babylon rose (about 609-598 BC). It is a conversation with God: the prophet's cry of "Violence!" (1:2-4), God's answer that he is raising up the Chaldeans (1:5-11), a second protest (1:12-17), the vision at the watch (2:1-5), five woes against the plunderer (2:6-20), and a prayer-psalm of the LORD's march and the prophet's joy (3). Its best-known line is "the righteous will live by his faithfulness" (2:4), which Paul and Hebrews quote. A scroll from Qumran, the Habakkuk Pesher, comments on chapters 1 and 2 line by line.
sections.refs: Habakkuk 1:2-4; Habakkuk 1:5-11; Habakkuk 2:4; Habakkuk 3:17-19; Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:37-38

common: The book is a dialogue between the prophet and God, set when Babylon was becoming the power of the region.
Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted in Romans, Galatians and Hebrews.
uncommon: Some date the book to Josiah's reign (before 609 BC) or read it as a late composite.

sections.b: The Chaldeans (Hebrew Kasdim) were a people of southern Babylonia. Nabopolassar, a Chaldean, founded the dynasty that ruled Babylon from 626 BC, and his son Nebuchadnezzar took Judah's kings captive. Habakkuk is the book that most fully describes them: bitter and hasty, fast as leopards, mocking kings, their strength their god (1:6-11). In Daniel the word also names a learned class of astrologers and magicians.
sections.refs: Habakkuk 1:6; 2 Kings 24:1-2; 2 Kings 25:4-10; Jeremiah 25:9-12; Daniel 1:4; Daniel 2:2

common: The Chaldeans are the Neo-Babylonian dynasty of Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar.
uncommon: Duhm (1906) proposed changing "Chaldeans" to "Kittim" in Habakkuk 1:6, which would mean the Greeks; few follow him.

sections.b: The Hebrew chamas means wrong done by force, often to the weak. It is the reason the LORD sent the flood (Genesis 6:11) and the word Job and Habakkuk cry out when no one answers. Habakkuk uses it for what Judah's powerful do and for what the Chaldeans do (1:2, 3, 9), and for the crimes the woes name (2:8, 17). Prophets and psalms ask God to end it; the Law gives it limits (Exodus 21-23).
sections.refs: Genesis 6:11; Job 19:7; Jeremiah 22:17; Habakkuk 1:2-3; Habakkuk 1:9; Habakkuk 2:8; Habakkuk 2:17; Micah 6:12

sections.b: In several old poems the LORD marches from the south at the head of armies, and nature breaks before him: Exodus 15, Judges 5:4-5, Deuteronomy 33:2, Psalm 68:7-8, Psalm 77:16-20 and Habakkuk 3. Cross and others have traced the pattern to the poetry of Canaan and Israel's earliest verse. The Bible keeps the vocabulary (sea, river, plague, Resheph) but gives it to one God without rivals. The pattern comes back in the New Testament at the Lord's coming (Revelation 19:11-16).
sections.refs: Exodus 15:1-18; Judges 5:4-5; Deuteronomy 33:2; Psalm 68:7-8; Psalm 77:16-20; Habakkuk 3:3-15; Revelation 19:11-16

common: The "divine warrior" poems share a pattern: march from the south, shaking of earth, defeat of sea or enemies, and rescue of the people.
uncommon: Some think Habakkuk 3 is among the oldest Hebrew poems; others date it to the prophet's own time.

sections.h: The pesharim: Qumran's commentaries on the prophets
sections.b: A pesher ("interpretation") is a commentary that quotes a prophetic text and says what it "refers to." The Qumran community wrote them on Isaiah, Hosea, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah and the Psalms. The Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab), copied about the late first century BC, is the best preserved: it covers Habakkuk 1-2 and reads the Chaldeans as the Kittim (a code for the Romans, or earlier Greeks), the wicked as the "Wicked Priest," and the righteous as the "Teacher of Righteousness." The identifications are the community's; scholars disagree about who the Priest and the Teacher were.
sections.refs: Habakkuk 1:5; Habakkuk 1:13; Habakkuk 2:2; Habakkuk 2:4; Habakkuk 2:5; Habakkuk 2:15-17

common: The pesharim read the prophets as speaking about the community's own times and leaders.
uncommon: The identity of the Teacher of Righteousness and the Wicked Priest is unsettled; proposals include members of the Hasmonean house.

sections.b: Habakkuk contrasts the swollen, crooked person with the righteous one, who will "live by his faithfulness" ('emunah: steadiness, reliability). The Greek makes it "my faithfulness" (God's), Paul quotes it without a pronoun for righteousness by faith (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11), and Hebrews makes it "my righteous one" who must not draw back (Hebrews 10:38). The Qumran commentary applies it to those loyal to the Teacher of Righteousness, and the Talmud finds in it the one principle behind the 613 commandments (Makkot 24a).

common: 'Emunah in Hebrew means steadiness; the Greek pistis covers trust, belief and faithfulness.
uncommon: Hays argues that "the Righteous One" in Paul's quotation may be Christ.

sections.b: Paul puts Habakkuk 2:4 at the head of his argument in Romans 1:17 and uses it again against reliance on the law in Galatians 3:11. Luther, Calvin and the Reformers took it as the verse for justification by faith alone; the Council of Trent held faith as the root of a justification that includes inward renewal; the Eastern church speaks of faith working through love. The card on Habakkuk 2 sets the churches side by side. Habakkuk himself has no doctrine of justification: the verse is about how the righteous live through danger.

Habakkuk asks God directly why he tolerates violence, and why he uses a guilty nation to correct a less guilty one (1:2-4, 12-17). The Bible lets the question stand through Job, Jeremiah, the Psalms and Habakkuk. God's answers in the book come in stages: the judgment is real (1:5-11), the plunderer will be paid back (2:6-20), the vision will come in its time (2:3), and the righteous must live steadily until then (2:4). The card on chapter 1 sets the churches' accounts of evil side by side.

Habakkuk 1:12 says God has appointed the Chaldeans to bring judgment and correction. Isaiah says the same of Assyria (Isaiah 10:5-15) and Jeremiah of Babylon (Jeremiah 25:9-14). The prophets add that the instrument is itself guilty and will be judged (Habakkuk 1:11; 2:6-20; Isaiah 10:12; Jeremiah 25:12). This is the Bible's usual way of joining God's rule and human responsibility.

Habakkuk never names Babylon. He says "the Chaldeans" (1:6) and describes an army, not a city. The five woes (2:6-20) are most often read as aimed at Babylon's empire, and Jeremiah 51:58 uses the same line about wasted labor against it (Habakkuk 2:13). Later readers used Babylon as a name for any oppressing power, as Revelation does for Rome (Revelation 17-18).

Habakkuk's "day of trouble" (3:16) and the march of the LORD (3:3-15) draw on the day of the LORD tradition, where God comes to judge and to rescue (Isaiah 13; Joel 2; Zephaniah 1). Whether the prophet means the Chaldean attack or a final day is debated. Zephaniah 1:7 and Habakkuk 2:20 share the call to silence before the LORD.

Habakkuk 2:3 says the vision waits for its time and will not be late, and 2:14 promises that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD's glory. Hebrews 10:37 reads 2:3 of Christ's coming. The Talmud uses it to warn against calculating the end (Sanhedrin 97b). The card on Habakkuk 2 gives the churches' readings of 2:14.

sections.h: The knowledge of the glory of the LORD
sections.b: Habakkuk 2:14 combines Isaiah 11:9 (knowledge of the LORD covering the earth like water) with Numbers 14:21 (the LORD's glory filling the earth), and in the middle of the five woes promises that violence will not have the last word. 3:3 says the earth is full of his praise.

sections.h: The LORD as warrior in Habakkuk 3
sections.b: Habakkuk 3 pictures the LORD going out to battle with a bow, arrows and spear, riding horses and chariots through the sea, and threshing the nations (3:8-15). Unlike the conquest narratives, Israel does not fight: the prophet watches and trembles. The poem shows how the Bible's war language was kept as praise and as a way to speak about God's rescue.

Habakkuk names three idols: the conqueror's strength (1:11), his net, to which he sacrifices (1:16), and the carved and cast image, a "teacher of lies" with no breath in it (2:18-19). The prophet's mockery follows Isaiah 44 and Jeremiah 10. The last woe is followed by the call to silence before the living LORD (2:20).

Habakkuk stands at his post on the tower to see what the LORD will say (2:1). The prophets often see themselves as lookouts (Isaiah 21:6-8; Ezekiel 3:17; Micah 7:7). Rabbinic tradition cites the verse of Honi the Circle-Drawer, who stood in a circle until it rained (Bavli Taanit 23a).

sections.h: Wine as a traitor and the cup of wrath
sections.b: In Habakkuk wine appears twice: as a traitor that unmakes the arrogant man (2:5) and as the means by which one man shames his neighbor, until the cup of the LORD's right hand comes around to him (2:15-16). The Qumran commentary quotes 2:5 with "wealth" in the place of "wine." The cup of wrath is a standing image in the prophets (Jeremiah 25:15; Isaiah 51:17).

sections.h: "The LORD is in his holy temple"
sections.b: Habakkuk 2:20 sets the silent idols beside the LORD in his holy temple and commands silence from the earth. Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13 use the same call. The temple may be Jerusalem's or the heavenly one (Psalm 11:4).

Habakkuk prays in two ways: the complaint of chapters 1 and 2 and the prayer-psalm of chapter 3, which is headed as a prayer and ends with a note for the music director. The prayer asks God to revive his work and remember compassion in anger (3:2), and ends with a vow of joy (3:17-19). The Roman, Byzantine and Jewish liturgies each sing it.

Habakkuk 3 has a title ("A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet"), the term shigionoth (as in Psalm 7), three selah marks (3:3, 9, 13) and a closing note "For the music director, on my stringed instruments" (3:19), like the notes in the Psalter. Its last verses echo Psalm 18 and 2 Samuel 22 ("feet like a doe's").

sections.b: In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar defeated the Egyptian army at Carchemish, which made Babylon the master of Syria and Judah's next ruler (Jeremiah 46:2). Habakkuk's date is argued from this: the Chaldeans of 1:6 may be rising just before it or on the march just after.

Jehoiakim ruled Judah 609-598 BC, put on the throne by Pharaoh Necho and then made to serve Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 23:34; 24:1). Jeremiah's woe against the king who builds his house by injustice (Jeremiah 22:13-17) is the nearest parallel to Habakkuk's woes of 2:9-12. Many commentators place Habakkuk's complaint in his reign.

Habakkuk does not name Nebuchadnezzar, but most readers identify his army with the "bitter and headlong nation" of 1:6. Jeremiah calls him "my servant" (Jeremiah 25:9). His inscriptions boast of cutting Lebanon's cedars, which may lie behind "the violence done to Lebanon" (2:17).

Habakkuk 3:7 sets the tents of Cushan beside the curtains of Midian, trembling as the LORD comes. Cushan occurs only here; it is probably a form of Cush, a name for peoples of the south. The Greek has "Ethiopians." Moses' Cushite wife (Numbers 12:1) lived in the same part of the world as Midian.

Midian lay in the northwest of Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba. Moses lived there (Exodus 2:15-22) and Gideon fought the Midianites (Judges 7). In Habakkuk 3:7 its tent curtains shake as the LORD comes from Teman.

The first complaint turns on one word: mishpat, "justice," comes out twisted (1:4). The Chaldeans bring their own "justice" (1:7), and the LORD appoints them for judgment (1:12). The woes pronounce the verdict on those who gain by injustice (2:9, 12).

Habakkuk is eighth in both the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk) and the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum, Habakkuk). Nahum comes before it in both. Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7 share the call to silence; Habakkuk 3 and Zephaniah 1 both have the day of the LORD.

Habakkuk joins two forms of the funeral and complaint tradition: the personal lament ("How long?", 1:2) and the woe (hoy, 2:6, 9, 12, 15, 19), which was the cry at a burial. The woes announce the plunderer's death while he lives.

sections.h: The sun and moon in Habakkuk 3:11
sections.b: Habakkuk 3:11 has the sun and moon "stand still" at the flash of the LORD's arrows. The verb is that of Joshua 10:12-13. Some link the verse to Joshua; others read it as the sky's response to a storm.

sections.h: The cup and anger in Habakkuk
sections.b: Habakkuk 3:2 asks that the LORD remember compassion in his anger, and 2:16 has the cup of the LORD's right hand come around to the plunderer. Anger is the LORD's answer to violence in Habakkuk, and compassion is what the prophet asks for the people.
Habakkuk 2:5 says the arrogant man opens his throat wide as Sheol and is like death, never full. The picture is also in Isaiah 5:14 and Proverbs 27:20; 30:15-16.

Habakkuk's book is called an "oracle" (massa') that he "saw" (1:1), and the LORD tells him to write the "vision" (chazon) on tablets (2:2). The prophet is both seer and respondent. The test of a true vision is that it comes (2:3; Deuteronomy 18:21-22).

Habakkuk 3:13 speaks of the LORD going out to rescue his anointed; the Greek has "your christ." Habakkuk 2:3 in the Greek speaks of "the coming one" and Hebrews 10:37 applies it to Christ. Whether the Hebrew means a king, the people or the Messiah is open.

Paul ends his sermon at Pisidian Antioch with Habakkuk 1:5 in the Greek ("See, you who sneer!"), where the Hebrew has "look among the nations." The Greek may reflect the Hebrew word for "traitors," the reading of the Qumran commentary.

Hebrews 10:37-39 joins Habakkuk 2:3-4 to a call to endure: the readers are told they are not people who draw back to destruction but people of faith. Habakkuk's own point is that the righteous live steadily while the vision waits.
Habakkuk 3:2 asks that the LORD remember compassion in his anger, as the creed of Exodus 34:6-7 holds the two together.
Habakkuk 2:7 calls the plunderer's creditors "biters" (noshekha), from the root that gives neshek, "interest." The nations he owes will wake and call in the debt.
The second woe (2:9-11) is against the one who gains by wrong for his house, to set his nest on high. The beam and stone of the house cry out against him.
Mary's song ends a line with "God my Savior," the words of the Greek of Habakkuk 3:18. The Greek of Habakkuk 3 is itself one of the canticles sung in the church's morning prayer.

Habakkuk is a good case for textual study. Two Dead Sea scrolls of the Twelve (Mur88 and 4Q82) agree with the Masoretic Text in what they preserve; the Septuagint differs widely in chapter 3 and in 2:4; the Habakkuk Pesher from Qumran quotes the text with a few variants of its own; and the rabbis recorded a "correction of the scribes" at 1:12. The variant entries on each of these are in the book.
Habakkuk 3:17 lists the failures of fig, vine, olive, field, flock and herd that the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 threaten. The prophet takes the whole list and still chooses joy.
Habakkuk 1:14 undoes Genesis 1:26-28: human beings are "like the fish of the sea," with no one to rule over them.
